To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the emptiness of a graph with n states can be decided by a probabilistic algorithm using O(n) bits of random-access memory and O(n) bits for the input; and (2) the emptiness problem for the graph product of a program and a property is solved in the same memory bounds.

the emptiness problem of a graph of n states can be solved with O(n) bits of random memory, and that the probability of error can be made as small as desired by increasing the size of the random memory.

the emptiness problem of nite automata over innnite words (i.e., B uchi automata) is solvable in O(n log n log log n) time and O(n) bits of memory (with some probability of error) and that the same is true for the emptiness problem for nite automata with two-way nite words as inputs.

the problem of verifying that a nite-state program satisfies some temporal property.

the problem of verifying temporal properties of n-ite state programs is in the class of problems solvable in expected polynomial time with respect to the number of states in the program and the number of states required to describe the property, but not with respect to the size of the property.

the algorithms presented in this thesis are the best possible algorithms for the problem of emptiness testing of nite automata with respect to the memory requirements, the time requirements, and the probability of error.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, given an error probability 1=2, we present algorithms for the emptiness problem of a graph of O(n) states that require O(n) bits of memory and run in O(n) time.
we present algorithms which can verify temporal properties of nitenite-state programs with a memory of size O (n), while the presently known algorithms use memory of size O( n log n) bits.

, given a nite-state program P and a property P, we can design a randomized algorithm that, with probability at least 1 2, decides whether the property P is satised or violated by the program P, using a memory of O(n) bits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the memory requirement of the emptiness algorithm can be made independent of the size of the product graph, as long as the algorithm is allowed to err with some small probability.
, in many cases, we can achieve a substantial reduction of the memory requirements by trading some probability of failure for a reduction of the memory usage.
the problem of verifying temporal properties of niteness-state programs is in the complexity class BPP.
